parsed.notes: Reviewed all five group_inventory assertions under Lens A only; no external sources used.

reasons: Lake identity gives case_name as A Quantity of Copies of Books v. Kansas, court U.S., court_level scotus, date_decided 1964-06-22, and year 1964.
Lake citations list official 378 U.S. 205, parallel cites 84 S. Ct. 1723 and 12 L. Ed. 2d 809, and vendor neutral 1964 U.S. LEXIS 823.

defect.evidence_quote: A seizure of all copies of the named titles is indeed more repressive than an injunction preventing further sale of the books.
defect.problem: The core procedural proposition is supported, but the holding is phrased too broadly. The opinion concerned seizure of all copies of specified/named allegedly obscene titles from P-K under a title-specific warrant, and Brennan's procedural rationale was a plurality/judgment opinion. The phrases 'every copy' and 'general seizure' should not read as all expressive-material seizures or a nonparticular general-warrant holding.
defect.proposed_fix: Limit the holding to: a plurality/judgment opinion held that seizing all copies of specified allegedly obscene titles from P-K under an ex parte warrant, before an adversary obscenity hearing, was constitutionally deficient.

reasons: The text supports constitutional deficiency because the warrant authorized seizure of all copies of specified titles and P-K had no prior adversary obscenity hearing.
The text states that the warrant "authorized the sheriff to seize only the particular novels identified by title in the Information," so 'general seizure' is loose at best.
The opinion identifies Brennan as announcing the judgment with three justices joining, while Black and Douglas concurred in the judgment on different grounds.
residual_risks: Rule statements should retain the plurality/rationale limitation when used outside the narrow facts.
reviewed.suggested_tightening: Replace 'general seizure' with 'seizure of all copies of specified titles' and add 'plurality/judgment opinion' to the holding field.

defect.evidence_quote: This is the teaching of Kingsley Books, Inc., v. Brown, 354 U. S. 436. See Marcus, at pp. 734-738.
defect.problem: The disclosed evidence does not support the home role 'Particularity — Historical / origin'. The opinion treats the rule as following Marcus and Kingsley Books, and the operative defect is lack of a prior adversary obscenity hearing before mass seizure, not origination of a particularity doctrine.
defect.proposed_fix: Change the role to 'Historical / application' or 'Historical / related' for expressive-material seizure procedure, or supply disclosed taxonomy evidence showing why this case is an origin case for Particularity.

reasons: The opinion expressly builds from Kingsley Books and Marcus rather than presenting itself as the origin of the rule.
The warrant was title-specific; the case is primarily about prior adversary hearing and expressive-material seizure safeguards.
residual_risks: The case may still belong on a Particularity page as a related historical application, but 'origin' is not supported by the disclosed files.
reviewed.suggested_tightening: Use a non-origin role unless the Particularity page or a disclosed taxonomy source establishes the origin classification.

reasons: The content frontmatter treatment fields match the lake treatment record: field_i_validity unverified, null as_of fields, composite_basis unverified, varies_by_point false, and the same scope note.
Lens A does not assess treatment/currency merits.
residual_risks: Treatment and good-law status remain for Lens B.
